speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Before I was born, there really the history of Viola and community. First it wasn't Viola, it was Palouse Bridge. And people lived here from everywhere. They came early and then stayed late. There was lots of different ones. The earliest settlers were the Palmers and the Loweries and the Scotts and the Griswolds. Griswold was a, well shall we say he was a squaw man. He married a princess of the Nez Perce tribe. And he moved farther back, all the time farther back. Finally he got up to what we call Griswold Camp now, but that was Griswold's meadow. He lived there with his wife and his children until the country commenced to get so settled up that people were coming by there and the miners were coming in. So he moved farther back, farther back, till everyone lost track of them entirely. But it was always Griswold Camp. Well that got cut down to Griswold Camp and Grizzly Camp it is now today. My earliest recollection of Grizzly Camp was dad and the family always liked to go up there to camp and fish. Whenever it was vacation time we always went to Grizzly Camp.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: One day we were camped there. I think it was an overnight camp, but early in the morning a man and a wagon, two men and a wagon came rumbling down across the bridge and over into the meadow. Pretty soon we heard a shot… dad said, well I guess they must have got something. Pretty soon they came back and they butchered a beef and they brought us a water bucket… full of liver and heart and a few pieces of good meat along with it. And they said, well maybe you'd like these. We can't seem to use them because we're just taking the meat on back home and we don't like the liver and the heart and the other pieces we've given you and here's some good steak to go along with it. That turned out to be Mr. Sexson and Lemon, the big cattle people of that country. They ran cattle all over the country then. It was Meadow Creek and Beeson Meadows and Grizzly Camp Meadow all the way down across and they had their big meadows over on Meadow Creek.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Dad liked to go fishing. Every year he'd plan a fishing trip just as soon as he got the garden in and the apples all sprayed just before haying time. It was always rainy then but that didn't matter. It was all the more fun. He'd put a big cover on the wagon and we'd all pile in. Sometimes the hired men would go along or the hired girl too. Always the family would come and stay with Dad about the time he got ready to go for a vacation and they had learned to take care of everything. They'd milk the cows and take care of everything until we got back. Sometimes Dad would stay as long as a month fishing and camping all up and down the Palouse River over into the Saint Maries and the St. Joe. One time he traveled as far up the St. Joe River as Boney Mountain and there we camped at Reed's Place, an old man that Dad had known for years.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: The boys climbed the top of Boney Mountain. They had a spyglass and they could see all over the country clear way down here. But you know, they left the spyglass up there and no one ever went back after it. When we were on the trip one time we stopped at an old man's place that had bees. They called him Honey Jones. He had a beautiful place and orchard and a beautiful little cave down by a falls they called Honey Jones Falls. Mother went down and sat in the shade and talked to him and his wife and they had a great visit. Got some honey from him, enjoyed his place very much. After a while we heard years later that he had given his place to the park, to be a park and then there would never be anything that would harm his falls. He'd always wanted that falls to remain just as it was. And years later we went up in 1957 or eight I believe it was and took the children, the grandchildren with us and we explored that park and the falls and it was very much the way it was when I had seen it when I was just a little girl.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Many years ago when the first miners came through the country there were lots of meadows and fishing was wonderful. But then after they muddied up the streams and taken all the game that they could get,… now there weren't just a few miners. There were hordes of them. The country wasn't the same… old Griswold,… he'd shake his head and he'd say, no good, no good. And he'd go on when he got enough skins from his beaver trapping but he done pretty well anyway. Then the loggers came in and they took off the timber, the mill was at Palouse City over the hill from Palouse Bridge. And the first mill was a big dam and it was a water wheel affair. And they saw quite a few logs there at Palouse and made a lot of lumber and enough to build the town of Palouse and some of the country places were built up from Palouse lumber.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: There was a pottery there too, they made brick and plant pots and jars and ears and different things and jugs, lots of jugs for the wine and the moonshine. Yes, there was grapes grown in this country in the early days. Mr. Miller, a neighbor over across from Asher and Nancy Palmer, had about a half an acre of grapes and he made his wine. They were wonderful grapes. I can just remember seeing the grape vineyard there and watching. They pruned them all down until it looked like they were all cut off in the spring and then they all come out in the great big bunches of grapes. But no more. I don't believe there's any grapes in the whole Viola Valley. I know there's none up in the Palouse Valley up above Potlatch. How did Potlatch get his name? Well, there was Indians, a legend, the Palouse Indians especially, it was prevalent amongst them. Anything went wrong with them. They didn't do good on the hunt or maybe they did good on the hunt and they got a whole lot of game and a lot of pelts. They'd throw a potlatch.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: He'd put everything he had outside his teepee and give it away. That was a potlatch. That's how Potlatch town got its name because that was the Indian campground there. A big grove of beautiful trees. Well, when the mill decided to come in, they brought the mill on up there from Risley's Mill in Palouse. They brought it on up to the Potlatch grounds. Cleared off all the timber and put in a town there and that was Weyerhaeuser's Mill then. Potlatch Timber Protective Association went to work because they didn't like so much fires in the country. But they took off the timber off of the flat, off of the flat land and off of the low hills. You wouldn't realize that that country had been a well-timbered area at one time, but there were huge big trees, pines and cedars and tamarack and fir. And it must have been a very beautiful country. Up where the scout camp is now was quite a grove, too. It was a cedar grove, but they took those all out. Wasn't anything left but thornbrush.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: The three C boys came in and they built some of the buildings. They had torn down, I think, the last building now at the scout camp that was built from before the three C's. And they did their bit to remedy some of the mistakes that the loggers had made. They opened up the trails and fixed the roads better and tried to straighten it out a little bit. But that was the way it was in those days. They logged and they didn't care anything about how they left the things. They'd leave the timber, some they didn't like. They'd leave the logs laying out to rot. No one wanted the old logs that weren't good for saw logs. They couldn't use all that wood, they didn't think. Nowadays, I think they use more of the wood. Looking out of my window here toward the north and east, it used to be a timbered mountain. Now they've cut nearly all of the timber off. There's just one little patch of timber. But think, years ago there was orchards on the hillside, trees on the top of the hill and in the gulches. But now it's all bare. They've taken off the trees in the Viola Valley. It's gone. The apple trees are gone, the pear trees are gone, the prune trees are gone. There just isn't any of the old-time things left anymore. It doesn't seem even the houses of the homesteaders are almost all gone. There are maybe a few left that were homestead houses, but most are in huge big fields operated by one man or firm of men. And that is what has happened to the beautiful green valley that grandfather saw way back when Mullen was building his road.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: There was once a trail up over the mountain and once in a while you'd look out over the hill and you'd see a string of wagons come down. Well, there would be one, two, three, maybe a dozen, maybe more than that. One time when I was a little girl, I climbed up to the top of my favorite tree and sat on the tall branches and looked out up the road. Coming over the trail and down across the hill to the road were wagons. Lots of wagons. I counted as many as I could count, but I couldn't count them all. Mother said there were 50 wagons in that train. Someone had died back up in the mountains and they were bringing him down to the church here at Viola for the ceremony and then up to the cemetery at Viola for burial. But those wagons, there were so many, they couldn't put them up at the church. The village was full and they were full and when the procession started up to the cemetery, the last one to leave the church couldn't find room to go in the road because they were all crowded one wagon right after the other all the way up to the cemetery. That was Meeks's. They had a sawmill back in the mountains where they saw the lumber for the early settlers.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Their lumber helped to build this house we live in now. Meeks's Mill was where everybody went for lumber and in turn the Meeks Mill people would come down here and sample grandfathers and dads. Cherries and peaches and pears and apples. And they enjoyed the Palmer fruit. The Palmer Orchard was famous all over the country. We've contacted people lately that live way back over in Amida that said they used to come over here when they were little to pick fruit in Palmer's Orchard. They liked the fruit and they didn't have any other. So his orchards were very famous. Guesses, our neighbor had orchard, Chaney's had orchard, Williams had orchard. There was orchards all over the valley here. It was a good fruit section. Viola had grown to be quite a large city by the time I was four or five years old. I can just remember dad carrying me on his shoulder to watch the schoolhouse or church burn. They burned down the church and the mill, the grist mill, and the schoolhouse and the livery's table burned and even the hotel burned. Almost all of Viola burned out and the older buildings, well there's only one left of the original building belonging to Nichols down in the village now, but the others were gone. It was a beautiful town at one time. There was a big four or five story hotel and the big livery's table and the grist mill, the Wells Fargo Depot, the Wells Fargo barns where they kept their horses, and there was boarding houses and blacksmith shops and five saloons believe it or not. When Grandfather Maxwell moved over to Viola from Palouse, he went around and tried to solicit people to get rid of the saloons. Well, a lot of the people didn't like them because when the men would come to town and the boys would come to town, they'd get drunk and then they'd start crowdsing up and down the streets and scare people and sometimes they'd do damage. So, Grandfather was the first one to start to get rid of the saloons. It was a good thing too, I guess. Old Lady Sims, well she was foster first and then she married Sims, ran the boarding house and the wards ran the blacksmith shop and David's had a big store. Well, it was a saloon first and they turned it into a store. Afterwards, it would come to be Cassin's store and several different people owned that store. Now it's the Viola Tavern Saloon. In those early days, they called them saloons. Now they're taverns. I don't know if they ever had any dancing girls here in the saloons or not. I never heard Grandfather say or Mother never told me about it either. But their big buildings, the big grist mill they had where they ground corn that people would raise and wheat for flour. Didn't have to take it all to Palouse when they had the grist mill here. It was run by horsepower and the boys would run around and round behind the horses or mules and grind the corn and they'd wheat that they had to grind for feed and for flour. One day one of the boys was grinding and grinding and he got tired and he tried to get someone else to do it but nobody would do it. So the next day, Mr. Beasley brought his girl down to grind the corn and she drove the horsepower and drove it and drove it and drove it. Finally, she tripped and she had sacks around her legs instead of overshoes. It was cold weather in the winter and she got tangled up in the tumbling rod and she was killed. One of the boys jumped in to help and his leg was hurt too and he only had one leg. His name was John Rothwell. After that they called him Peg Leg Rothwell. But they stopped the grist mill then. They said, well that was just enough. They wasn't going to do it anymore. It was soon after that that the mill was burned down. I've often wondered if maybe some patriotic citizen didn't want anybody else getting hurt on it and they set fire to it but no one ever knew. Then the church burned and the schoolhouse burned. They accused the little boy of setting the fires but everyone knew he didn't because he was scared to get out in the dark and he was a very timid little boy too.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: But that was Stekker. The little boy was a nice little boy. These folks finally sold out and moved because they couldn't stand the talk about their boy setting the fire to the town and burning it up. The folks always had lots of cattle. Uncle Wes had a huge ranch and a huge bunch of cattle. He never knew just how many cows he did have or horses. He raised horses for the cavalry and he had Morgan stallions from the government and the bell founder mares. So he raised pretty nice horses. They were almost all the same color. Bay with white stockings and a star in their forehead with black mane and tail. Beautiful horses and fast too. One day he decided that he'd go down to the village of Colfax. Viola wasn't very big then. That was before Viola became very much of anything except just Palouse Bridge and a post office. I think someone had built a little bit of a store down here by the name of Knapp.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Anyway, Wes hooked up his team or had his driver hook up the team rather. He always had a driver to drive his buckboard. He didn't like to drive himself. He wanted to look around and see what was going on. And Wes never drove a team that wasn't right up on their hind legs ready to run. Most always they were fresh horses off the range and maybe had never been driven before. Jeff Hill was the driver. Usually after he got big enough to drive. He drove Wes's team everywhere all over the country. But this day Wes wanted to go to Colfax in a hurry. So they drove down to Colfax and on the way they met another neighbor that was going to Colfax. I don't know maybe it was tax time or something. They were going down for some kind of a meeting. It was George Hill. And he yelled at Wes and says, Come on, Wes, let's go. And they raced all the way to Colfax. They got down there. Jeff said they blanketed their horses and he rubbed the horses and worked with them while they went up to the meeting that they had. And on the way back where they raced the horses again and when they got home, he had to rub the horses down and blanket them and walk them to keep them from getting stiff.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Then one time,… dad had a team that Wes had given him, one that Wes had driven quite a few different times and they were quite tame. See my dad had a lame shoulder and a lame arm and he didn't do very much driving. It was very wild horses. He was driving this team around and oh he could go places so fast in that team. I don't remember just what their names were. We'll have to try to find out from someone else and remember what dad's team was. But anyway, the hired man wanted to take the team to go to Colfax to the dance. Dad said, All right, you handle them careful and be sure to blanket them when you get down there. And don't let them go too fast. So the hired man drove the team down to Colfax and hooked him up to the hitching rail in front of the dance hall, forgot all about blanketing him. He had his girl with him. And then after a while when the dance was over, the wee small hours of the night, they danced all night in those days. It had been cold and those sweaty horses that had to stand out there all night long in the cold, they weren't used to that. They were used to being blanketed. Well, he drove them back home, but they were pretty stiff. They weren't going too good. He was pretty badly frightened by the time he got them home and put them in the barn and he put blankets on them after he got them back in the barn and worked with them a little bit. Next morning, Dad went out to see about his horses and he noticed that they were all stiff and stove up.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: No good, he said. Turn them out. We'll just turn them back out in the pasture. They won't ever be any good anymore. They were what they called foundered. I don't just exactly understand it, but it seems like if a horse gets real hot and then gets cold, well, they get so they're stiff and stove up. Well, we call arthritis in human beings, I guess. Uncle Wes's teams were wild and his drivers were wild. He had about 40 hands, cowboys, that rode with him, done his riding and took care of his stock for him. Clear down to the Rattlesnake Hills, the horse heaven country was his horse pasture and his little pasture took in about all of what's south of Viola around the hill in the cup. It was a huge big spring there where he'd water his stock. When he'd bring in the horses to sort out what he wanted for the government, he'd put them in that little pasture. It was 100 acres or so of pasture that was well fenced with high rail fence.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Then he'd ship the horses out or they'd take them down to the Fort Walla Walla and sell them for the cavalry remounts. Along about 1915, he decided there just wasn't room enough for him anymore. They fenced up a lot of his pasture down below Colfax. There was fenced in around the poplars and the wells and they fenced in around the little towns as they went down. And the people had pretty well fenced up all the good grass. So he rounded up all his stock and his horses and his cows. He had four trainloads of them and he shipped them to Canada. And here at Viola, he loaded on his family and all of his housewares and his tools and implements. Some of his pet stock that he had, his fancy bulls and his real good stallions and his mares that he had that were quite tame. He brought some over to Dad. There was Ned and Fred and Len and Joe and Patch.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And Dad had another one he called Nell. And Susie was a little gray colt that had gotten crippled up on the racetrack. They were going to shoot her, but Dad saw her and he said, well, we'll just see what we can do doctoring her up. I petted her and petted her and he called her my horse because I doctored her and helped pet her so much and took her carrots and water and she went down and she'd stand in the creek. She was just a little cold. I think maybe might have been a short yearling. But that was the team that Dad drove, the Susie and Nell. There was Patsy was another one that Wes let Dad have. And all of those horses that were tame and nice, Uncle Wes gave to Dad for Dad needed the horses on the ranch here to work. The others were shipped to Canada. No, he didn't sell many of his horses. He turned what he could over to the army at Walla Walla, the court. Then he shipped the rest of them up to bigger Saskatchewan and started to drive. Jess told about it not too long before he died because Jess was getting up into 80 years of old before he told me this story. But anyway, when they got to Canada and to bigger, they found a place to camp out and they decided they'd stay there for a little while. So he stayed there for several years and run the wheat branch. But the cattle and the horses went on to the Peace River.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Way over across the tundra and Jess said it was the awfulest, meanest drive he ever saw in his life. But he drove west in the buckboard all the way across. When you got to the tundra, you just didn't know whether you were going to drop down in Axle Deep or whether you were going to go on. There was no roads. They went along ahead of the cattle and the horses. If they'd gone behind them, they might have had a muddy earth path because they drove from June until fall. When they got over the Peace River, though, it was a beautiful country and a wonderful rangeland. And there, Wes settled his cattle and his horses. And every now and then, Wes would come back down on the train to buy his fall clothes. One day, particular, the funny story my brother used to tell, they run, dad run a dairy at that time and the boys would take the milk to the depot every morning to go to Spokane.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And Wes went over to David's store in Moscow and bought his clothes for the winter. I think he had six or eight suits of underwear and two suits of clothes, a big bare skin coat, mittens and gloves and caps, socks, everything that he would possibly need all winter long. And he bought overshoes too. He put these all on the morning he was going back to bigger Saskatchewan up in Canada because he didn't want to pay duty on them and he would have had if he had no one of them. The boys said they had to help him into the buggy and they had to boost him onto the car to get on the train. But that wasn't the worst of it. He rode on past Spokane and clear up into bigger Saskatchewan. When he got there, there was a blizzard blowing. The livery stable man had his team. They helped him out of the train and helped him over to the livery stable and helped him up into the buggy and wrapped him up good with robes.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And they were buffalo robes too, Jeff said. And they even put hot stones in the bottom of his buggy. And then they went out and the blizzard was blowing so bad they tried to persuade him not to go. Now I want to get home, he said, and the horses will take me home anyway. So he started out down the road and he turned the horses loose when the blizzard got too bad and he tucked down under the robes. Well the horses went until they couldn't anymore and they got off in the lee of a hill and stopped and stood there. Well, Wes couldn't get out of the buggy to do anything about it. He was too clumsy with all his clothes. But it was a good thing he had his clothes on because the next day when the riders went out to hunt for him, they hunted at night but they couldn't find him. But the next morning early they all rode out there around to hunt for the boss. They found him, sound asleep under the robes. He wasn't frozen, there wasn't anything the matter with him. The horses were pretty cold but the horses were buried in the snow. The snow had just combed up over them and made a nice cover for the horses and the buckboard. After that, Wes never went out alone anymore. He always had a driver and Jeff was usually the driver until Jeff got sick. He didn't want anymore of that Canada so he came back down here to live on the hill ranch until he died.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Dad had quite a few horses if I can remember. To me by Ruby. She has a diary that belonged to my grandmother. Nancy Palmer. And way back in 1874 or something like that, she dated it and the time goes back to the time when Mullen was building a road and the 7th Cavalry was working in Montana. Uncle Wes was just a boy then and he was with the 7th Cavalry and the Army. And they were up in Montana getting ready to build a Mullen Road, surveying and making a country for white folks to sit in, to live in. They had time to go hunting a little bit now and then. The country was beautiful and full of game. There was few Indians but they were not at all bothering the people. Seems like that Custer's last den had been just about the last of it all and they weren't a bit worried about that. Uncle Wes just missed that because he'd been sitting on an errand over to the other side of the mountain and so that was the way it went.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Grandfather Ancher Palmer was an audience man. He drove a mule, carried a little lancet and a few little medical things to fix up things and he was called a doctor. Well he was an herb doctor so he went along with the Army and had a grand time along doing it too I guess. He enjoyed the country very much. When he left Missouri his friend gave him a package of apple seed, just a little buckskin bag he carried in his pocket. Mile after mile he wondered if he'd ever find a place to plant those apple trees. Well one day he was up in Montana and he packed up driving a six horse, six mule team. He didn't drive horses, it was mules. Got it all loaded up and raised it going. Bang. One of the mules kicked him right in the side of the head and hurt his eye. He couldn't see so he just hung up the lines and had the mules go hunt the rest of the Army. They followed, they were used to doing it so they did and after a while they caught up with some of the soldiers and they saw his predicament so they said on ahead for Uncle Wes, he was an Indian Scout at that time, and he came back and the captain said you guys better hit for home. That eye isn't going to be any good and you're not going to be any good to yourself or anybody else until you get it treated.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: So they started down the, over the mountains and down the corn lane, down the St. Joe River and Saint Maries River to the lakes and then over the hills until they came to the Palouse River and down over some more hills and came to a beautiful little meadow. White rock springs and trees around now and then and bushes and game. There were deer in the meadow and prairie chicken and then Uncle Wes looked around and he said here we'll camp. So he threw the sacks, the packs off of the mules and turned them loose to graze. I don't know whether he hobbled them or not. They didn't say in the old diary but I suppose they did. They didn't take much chances on being left alone in a strange country where it was hundreds of miles to anywhere. So then he dealt a fire, fixed the ampoule comfortably and told him to take a nap and eat it for all. See if he could find something to eat. First he got a deer and had some meat, a hodgepodge of it. Then he found the prairie chicken and blew it off first and he had the eggs and the chicken too. Well that made a stew. He looked around and he found some watercress in the spring and some docks and then some manioc roots and he made quite a stew. Resembled our own meat stew that we made nowadays with potatoes, manioc roots and such and he had some canvas bulbs too in that stew. He looked around and wandered around where our grandfather slept and he had his stew bubbling on the fire.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: It was a beautiful place and he thought oh how wonderful it would be to live here. But after a while when grandpa woke up he looked around and he said well that stew was awful good. This is a beautiful place. I'm going for a stroll up the hill. So he was around up on the hill and looked around and oh what a place. I'm going to plant my apple seed right here. So he did. He planted his apple seed. He said I'm coming back and going to bring the folks back. Went down and told Wes about it and Wes said I think so too. Let's get out of here and go. So they got up real bright and early in the morning and started out for Walla Walla. Fort Walla Walla. They got down there. I think it took them about a day to get there. It was real late. I think they camped down on the river that night. That would be the Snake River.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And they went across the Snake River and on down to Walla Walla the next morning. And there they decided they'd better take a boat on down because their father wasn't very well with that eye hurting. The doctor did it at the Fort Walla Walla. They came up a little bit. So they went on down to the raft of canoes. Down to where they could get a boat and go around and clear around that way around the horn of South America I guess. What Ruby said. And then down and up the Mississippi River again to Missouri to St. Hill. And then on over to where the folks lived in Illinois. And that was the end of the story. In 1870 Mrs. Bets and Grandpa decided to come back home to Asher Palmer. He called it home here at White Rock Springs. So he gathered the family together and Dad had the honor to guide the team. They started out with four nice horses but they didn't pull very good so Dad finally decided to get oxen. So he got two fans of oxen and he loaded on everything. If he went along he could do sister things. And Harriet. Her name then was Harriet Falter. She had two million children. Artie and Lily.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And they come on back across to Missouri to St. Joe. And they got there and they met up with some other wagon trains and they met a Mormon wagon train. And the Mormon wagon train, well that wasn't too good. Dad didn't like it so he said he was going to put Grandma and his sister on the train at St. Joe and go to San Francisco that way. And Harriet didn't though. She decided to go on with the Mormons and the wagon train. It was as though she wanted to or not. We don't know. Because later on she found out she didn't want to. But then that's another story. They got to San Francisco and then took a boat and went on up to the mouth of the Columbia River and on up to Oregon City. So they stayed for a year or so. And all they see there, Grandpa and the boys, Granddaddy, Uncle Wes and my dad went on up the river with some of his mother's relatives that were along with them. There was the Newgens and the Green.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: They come on up the river and clear up the Snake River even. And clear up the Almoda. There they stayed overnight and there was a winter weather. It was snow at the time they got there. And it was over one day Dad decided to go get the mail if there was any because there was an irritating force at the coast of the river. So he got his horse and he went on over the hill to the top of the hill and there was snow. And he said, we couldn't go any farther so he tied his horse on top of the hill and slid down the hill to the port to the trading coast and got the mail. Climbed back up with one letter and some head but that was the one that they had. He got a few things I think from the first day of the trip but their supplies were getting short. We went on back down to Almoda here. They were smithing in a little rock house. It was still down there. I believe we found the same old rock house that was still there when we were there just before we started the band.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: The next day they had stepped up their ponies and loaded everything onto a wagon that they had gone along with them on a raft. That must have been hard working those canoes and rafts all the way up that river but they had their seams kind of a tug or whatever it was that they steamboat that went paddle, paddle, paddle with a great deal in behind it. And that was what they come up the river with. They went all over land then. They're across to Colfax and they had two little dogs with them but they'd lost their fleas. Their fleas annoyed them but there wasn't any fleas left at all but they finally got the Colfax. Then they come on up here to Whitehouse and build a cabin. First thing they did. And they got the cabin off except so they could go back after grandma and Emma. And then Harriet can come out at that time. They build a house there and that's their house too. So there were two. So grandfather said it was too far to go to Colfax and stages were coming in pretty soon. So when grandma and the girls came the next year he decided to apply for a post office. So he did and they got his post office. But in 1875 there was a post office but he had his certificate from the government way back in Washington D.C. And we have it here today.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Then grandfather thought well the folks were all coming up. So he went down the river and brought grandma and Emma and them up so they got up here in 1875. And they had a full fledged post office here. They had brought over with them an old chest or a secretary they called it that had little pigeon holes in it. That was the post office. And grandfather kept the post office. But you know to go back the minute grandma got here she looked all around and they had set up a little baking stove so she could bake. And they were old pioneers iron stove. And lots of nice kindling around her. She said I'm going to cook some dinner. And she went around and she saw grandpa's apple trees and they were just loaded with apples. There was early apples this was in July I think or August. There was early apples and there would be a lot more later on. But she made the most wonderful apple pie. It was down in the diary that Ruby our cousin had before their house burned up and she told us about it. That apple pie from the White Rock Springs farm. Oh they didn't know what to call it. They looked around and it was Palouse Bridge the government had said well it's Palouse. Can't be in the bridge he says. Palouse Bridge as far as we know. And that was where people got their mail. There was all kinds of neighbors around by then. It was settling up fast. People had found how beautiful Palouse was and the Indians weren't bothering and they were friendly and nice. Now I'll have to go back and tell you a story about grandma Maxwell when the next book came out.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Grandma Maxwell both grandpa Maxwell James Allen Maxwell and Lucy Nugent were married back in 1816. Grandma was born in 1866 and in 1865 she was going to see just a baby when they decided to come out here. It was after the war and grandpa had got home from the war and he decided that there wasn't anything to do but to get right out of where they were and come out here. So they left their part of the country there in Indiana and started out. Of course it was a pushcart and then they lived in a little sod house for a while. You see they started back before while they were in Ohio and then they started out. That was pretty good. Then they stopped. That was a nice little place and he built a little sod house. There was a hole in the ground and put the sod up on top and made a little sod house. And they stayed there all that winter. The next spring they planted a garden and they had flowers and they even had a cow.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And they just got along real good. The next year after that Aunt Ollie had been born and they thought well it's fine till they winter again. But that winter the wind blew so hard and it was so snowy that it was a blizzard. And the blizzard blew so hard that grandpa had a big roll of twine and he unrolled that twine to go find the cow out at the barn. They couldn't see the barn at all and the blizzard blew so hard. And that prairie country was terribly hard to get around in when it blew. And then blew and blew and blew. But he got to the cow, fed water to her and milked her and brought the milk back so the babies could have milk. Rose and Ollie had their milk. Then the spring came and they planted the garden again. But this time all of a sudden all the noise they ran outside and there was grasshoppers everywhere. The grandpa was just a little girl then. I think she was about eight. She covered up the flowers and they tried to save things and they got those little things in the garden. But the grasshoppers ate everything.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: They turned the little in the garden and the radishes. They did little things down in the ground. The hay was all gone. There wasn't anything even the grasshoppers were trying to eat the pinks up. And all the things that got her just wasn't anything left. Even the flowers and grammars brushed and brushed and brushed to try to keep the grasshoppers off of her finally eating up. Well they were disturbed. Grandpa said, well, we haven't anything to eat and we haven't anything to do so let's go. Go to Oregon. They passed us everything and we went on over to where the railroad was and got on the railroad train and immigrant train. And they had all their belongings in their car and they could cook in the car and eat and just be a family. And they got acquainted with Rowan and Mrs. Rowan lived in the car right next to them. So they had a good time coming out. But somehow or other, oh yes, I forgot there was another baby born back here in that grasshopper in his time. His name was Eldon. Eldon picked me myself.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And Uncle Eldon dropped something on his toe and it was sore. And little boys at that time, two years old, wore apron or dresses, little boy dresses, tore down and he'd gather up things in his apron and pack them around. And he'd go along and he'd say, throw a toe or anything. Gonna do it anyway. He was a really, really little pioneer boy. He could just get right along. So we got the transom fixed up. They got off the train and they loaded onto an immigrant boat. Gonna take them up to the Oregon country. They rode steerage and sawdust on the floor. And when they got out to sea, Grandpa made Grandma and the children all lay down till they got clear way out to sea. And then he let them get up and go out and they could look around. People were so appreciative they could hardly stand it to stay downstairs.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: But they went around, they looked down and there was a funny thing going on. What was that? It was a turtle. They caught a big sea turtle and the sailors were cutting it up to make turtle soup. Well, that was going to be a change from the beans and salbella, as they called it. And they dried soup and things that they had aboard. It wasn't anything like we have now for food. They had a hard pass to that sea biscuit, they called it. My mama made that turtle soup and it was so good, but it was green. My mother says she could remember that green turtle soup. But oh, how good it was. They had turtle soup then for four or five days. And finally they got clear up to the mouth of the Columbia River and they went over to the Oregon City. It was Portland, but there was a little wood chopping place there. And Grandpa got a job chopping wood for the boat. They lived there for a while. And they moved into another pretty cabin in the north.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And there was a beautiful meadow and there were sheep all around. But there was one apple tree right close to their house. They had loaded with apples and they were all over the ground. Uncle Elton had never seen an apple before. And he gathered up apples and he'd open and he'd go around, throw it to her or anything, throw it to her or anything, go and pick those apples up anyway. He was going to have applesauce. And so he went and carried the apples up. And that was Ewing's place. Mr. Ewing came down and he gave them milk and cream and they had meat. But he chopped wood. Grandpa chopped wood there before they were boat for two or three years. Before they finally decided to come on up to the police country. Then they boarded the boat. They had regular steamers then going up the river. They put all their things and their little dogs on the boat. They'd get in their cow and some chickens. And they come on up to Wallula. There they got off their boat and they had brought along their horses too. And they got off and unloaded their wagon and all their things and put them in and headed over for Colfax. That was the place to go. There wasn't any place else. Of course they could go over to Fort Walla Walla but they didn't. They went to Colfax. They got to Colfax and then on up.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: They didn't know exactly where to go but there was a place called Eibler's Wretch where a man could cut rails and wood and things for the settlers. And he thought well I'll cut enough rails to hump. Since my home's dead before I try to hump it. So he went out and they lived there for two years while he cut rails. Sold some to the neighbors for supplies. He got turnip seed, potatoes and meat from Mrs. Rowland. He had a farm over where he's Moscow now but they call that Paradise…  and they lived there and their grandma was learning to read. She was nine years old. And Aunt Ollie and Uncle Eldon. Finally he got enough rails cut to go and get his big place there. They went down where it's Whalum now and they sent their homestead there. And got it all the rails built. Everything going in that wheat and oats and barley in there. Cows were doing well in their teens and mom was going to be a good size girl then. But she had a horse she called Gipp. And she'd ride all over the country to visit places. She'd go to school at Fallon. They had quite a nice little school there. In the summertime they'd go down and kick service berry down on the three-fork. That's Pullman now.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And when she got to be a pretty good size girl all of a sudden it actually happened. Grandpa was still cutting rails. He had fallen in some way and broke it late. So Grandma had to see the boy and family. And Grandma and Aunt Ollie done the chores and neighbors came in and helped. They got the thrashing done and everything old. All the neighbors would come in with everything to help when somebody got hurt in those days. There wasn't any doctors so that was the way they lived. Then fall mom had to go to school. She got through the day cold school there. She went to Collins School a while and got attended with J.R. Collins and some more of the boys. But then she was about 12 or 14. Had to go to Moscow. Moscow had a little village then and they had a college there. High school. There she went to college there for three years.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And then she taught the Collins School first year. Well we don't want to forget Uncle Wes. He and Grandfather were always wandering around and going places and doing things. One time they were hunting way out in the mountains. They'd been prospecting around for some more timber to make shakes with and to make rails and posts. Grandfather's ranch and Uncle Wes's ranch were progressing rapidly. But they were camped out there. One evening they decided that we're going to home the next morning. And they didn't have any food to eat only just some dried prunes. And Uncle Wes said well our bank's a fire tonight and put those prunes in the little iron pot. And we'll have prunes for breakfast anyway before we head for home. So we chugged them up real good. Then he rolled up in his buffalo robe. They used the buffalo robe instead of sleeping bags. And they went to sleep. But Uncle Wes wasn't quite as sleepy as Grandfather was and he kind of left his one eye open. He chugged them under his buffalo robe and walked. And here come a kite.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: He come down and he spoke around and all the places even took hold in. The buffalo robe and kite to pull it off of him but it didn't pull so he went around. Finally he went up to the fire which had died down. Now there's just barely a bunch of anchors that were warm. He looked to see why it wasn't smelling good. So he sniffed at it a while and pawed at it. Finally she kind of leaped down in with her nose and rooted around and pulled the lid off. Well that was better yet because she stick her nose down in there and she got a prune. Mmm that was good. She licked her chops and ate two or three of them. Then she covered the pot back up and even raked some sticks and things up over the lid. Mr. Ray raced off into the woods. Uncle Wes watched and pretty soon used to come back. Two little baby tyrants were with her. Oh they were two puppies. And she brought them right up to the kettle and she opened the kettle again and gave each other a prune to eat. Then she covered it all up again and away they went into the woods. But Aunt Tiamo for Wes was so interested that he made still to watch. But it was getting daylight and almost no more.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: When they got home that trip they told the story of what had happened and asked Grandma for something to eat. Grandma said, oh now Wes. And his wife and the other girls and Emma said, Wes that's just one of your tall tales. Oh no it isn't, said Grandfather. We didn't have much breakfast. I'll tell you that much. We're hungry. Got something for us to eat Ma? Just any old thing will do. And that was the end of that story. Many many years they told that story and laughed about it. How the coyote got Grandpa and Wes his dead breakfast… then there was another story that was interesting. Grandfather Maxwell had just gotten… a little bit of a headache. He was an old gentleman and his wife was at home and he didn't like it one bit but he had to be out there… he wanted to go home off to bed because he heard that the baby was sick. Well it didn't seem to make any difference to anybody else about his baby. So he had to go along anyway. As they went along down the road they were following down after the southern soldiers going on Sherman's big march to the sea. As they went along there were rails along the fence and it was rainy and bad weather. And they,… sherman asked his orderly to go and tell the lady that they would camp there and to promise that he'd only take just the top rail. Each soldier would be obliged to build a campfire so they could cook their supper. All they had with them was hardtack and what they could forage. Sometimes they'd find cornbread, corn pone it was called, and bacon. And they'd slice the bacon and heat the corn pone by their fire and they had their hardtack along with them. Well that was just fine. That night they had a big feed and everybody was so happy around the bonfires. But the next morning when they started off down the road Grandpa looked through the basement. There was only one rail on the ground. The rest of the rails were all gone. But he went to the General Sherman and he said, General, I told the lady we'd only just take the top rail.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: General looked around and he called to his captain and some of the others and he said, what's the comment on the rest of those rails? Well captain, there's only just this. Every man took the top rail and when they got to the last man there wasn't anything left but the bottom rail. And that was that. Then another time there was a story that was interesting to me. I was real thrilled about it when they told it. Grandpa sat down with me one day. I was only five or six years old but I remember him telling the story so vividly. He was running. It was raining and it was muddy and he was running just as hard as ever he could run. And something was following him. It was retreat. Everybody was either run or get captured by the southern soldiers. Oh no, he was a blue-bellied yank and he had to run. So he ran and he ran and he ran and he got so tired he couldn't go another step. Sat down beside a tree, a great big old oak.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: And he said, all right, here's my meetings. I'll get it but I can't help it. I can't run another step. So he held his breath and listened. Something came right up to him and he sniffed, sniffed, sniffed. Felt up with his hand and there was two great big ears. It was so dark he couldn't see but he felt around and well, if it wasn't the old army mule, the one that he used to pet and drive once in a while. Well, he got on the mule and they ran through the rain and walked and walked until finally they caught up with the rest of the troops. And then he was kitted about being so slow and, well, what in the world are you so white about and what's the matter anyway? You're all wet and draggled and here you come in riding old gray. Well, I was scared and I thought he was an enemy soldier and he was going to bay at me, baying at me every minute and there he was.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Right behind me I could have caught a line and roll but I didn't. Only just this last little wave. And that was the story about the mule. Another time Grandpa told the story about they kept beside a little hill. It was rainy and cold and they all built fires around. This time it was right in the woods so they had lots of wood. And pretty soon the word was passed around, don't get close to that hill, it's turpentine. It's pitched from the trees. This is the turpentine forest to make turpentine out of this stuff. All right, we'll be careful. Everybody had a nice fire and they put a little piece of pitch on their fire to make it burn real good… it was fun that night. They were smooth, moon was smooth, going all the way and the trees were nice and sheltered. Nobody was having anything but a good time. They'd gone over to an old big farmhouse where there was some negroes and the negro mammy had baked them some corn pones for the general. Grandpa had corn pone that night as well as his other things to eat. And they got caught up with the provision wagon and bought some rice. When nobody knew how to cook it they had their little kiddos. And there was one boy,… he said, I'll cook the rice and you eat it. So he started cooking it. But first his little kiddo got too full and he borrowed another and another and another until everybody's kiddo was full of rice. Because rice swells, you know. Well the time he got through everyone in that platoon had rice. It was good but they learned how to cook rice. It only takes a little, you know. And they had used a whole lot.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Then the next morning when they went off down the road, marching down toward the sea, Grandpa looked down the side of the road and there was a seeming stream of, can you guess? This hill had gotten on fire some way and all the fish was melting and running down the side of the road in the ditch. And that was a waste but they couldn't help it. Now to get back to this part of the country again… well they had gotten the stages in and the stages were run by Jap and Green Chambers that had come up with Moscow. To Moscow with Grandpa Maxwell. And they had a grand time. They had coyote horses that they'd gotten from the Indians and they run the horses to get, hurry up and get there fast. And then they'd keep them in pastures at different places. At Grizzly Camp for one place and then over at Green's little ranch way back up in the mountains, that's where our cabin is now. And then they'd back and forth with their stage and they enjoyed their freighting and the stage driving. One day,… green told the story.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: He had a passenger. This time it was a Chinese gentleman. He had a long queue that came clear down to his hips and he wore a long black coat. They skinned him and hung him up behind the cookhouse and they were going to have bear steaks to suffer that night. Well, the gentleman saw that and the cook was cutting off steaks and he was there. He run back, hunted up Jap and he said, or Green, and he said, Get me out of here! Get me out of here! Quick! They're eating human beings! I can't stand that! Get me out of here! I just can't stay here! I don't want to eat human beings! They'll be eating me next! Green laughed and he said, Oh, come on, let's go see. They went on around the, to the cookhouse and looked, took a look and Green said, Oh, it's a bear! And he rolled over and over and over in the grass, tumbling, laughing and laughing until he couldn't stand up. He says, Come on, I'll show you. And he hunted up the bear's head and the bear's skin and the claws and cut off some of the claws for the Chinaman and the Chinaman got acquainted with the wild, wild west. No, they didn't eat men. They ate bear and he liked the bear too. The next day they took him on up to green, the end of the stage line where he found a Chinese coolies that were working the mines up on China Hill. We were up on China Hill several years ago and the diggings are still visible and way back up on top. You can see their little low cabins that they lived in. They're not completely rotted away yet and it's been over 100 years.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: When they come back, the Chinaman always collected every bit of their gold up every time he came in and he came in every month, regular. And then he'd take the gold back down to San Francisco. One day a story is told about mom's cousin, Bob Nugent. He worked on the stage mines, as you know, and he liked the Chinese whiskey. Those coolies make the best whiskey ever was, he said. And I'm going to get some tonight. It's not a bad night for it at all. Anybody going to help me? No, nobody wanted to go. You can go by yourself. Bob was a heavy drinker and he was a big man. He weighed around 300 pounds and he was over six foot eight tall and had curly red hair. So the legends tells us, of course, mom said he was a big man. He weighed around 300 pounds, all right, and he was taller than most everybody else. And he went up there that night, walked by himself, and they didn't say anything about they didn't hear him come back and they wondered what had happened. The next day they went exploring and found him laying in a ditch beside the road. He had a jug of his coolies whiskey, all right, and he drank all he could and had gotten drunk and laid down and gone to sleep. Well, they took him back down to Green's house, cabin, sobered him up, and he told the story. Those Chinamen, they got a million dollars worth of gold in that little black pot. Believe me now, I'm going to get that little black pot if I can. They got a million dollars in it. Well, Jaff and Green said they don't have it there very long. That Chinamen that comes in every month with a big long queue takes it back to San Francisco.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: No, Bob said, it's there. I know it's there. Well, nobody believed him. He'd just been dreaming. Maybe he'd seen some gold, all right, but the Chinamen with a long queue had taken it back to San Francisco. Even today, people come in now and then looking for that pot of lost gold of the Chinese. Old Bill Freeberry, our friend and miner of the hoodoos, said he had looked many, many times and other people had always come in looking for that lost gold… funny to look for it. Oh, I think there is, they said. So they went wandering around all over the hills and they wound up clear over the hills and over Gold Hill into Gold Creek,… into the Farmington country, and even wound up over in the Minerva-McCroskey Drive and Park, but they couldn't find that gold, that kettle. Evidently, the Chinamen had hit it too good or else there wasn't any kettle.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: To go back a few years from that, the folks were getting along real fine in their new homesteads. The orchards were going good and the wheat fields are going nicely and they were just having a lot of real good farmer good times. And all of a sudden, Grandma looked up and there come a rider with a foamy horse that just a-pounding the horse as hard as he could and riding and screaming, Indians, Indians, they're coming, they're going to scalp you. Grandma said, scalp us? Why, the Indians are friendly, what's the matter with you? Well, they're going to, they've got a trouble up there and mulling and around Spokane and Colville and all around up in there and they're going to come down here and scalp us all, we got to run to the fort quick. And he just beat it on as fast as he could go up pounding his horse and he couldn't go faster and faster till the poor horse can hardly go it looked like. Grandma said, well, I don't see what's the use and Grandpa said, well, what in the world? I don't see any sense. Indians are all nice and friendly around here. The only ones we ever see are the Palouse or the Spalding Indians and then the Fall, the others all come and they're just as friendly as can be. I'm not going to run to leave my place. And old lady rolling over toward Camas Meadows or the Paradise Valley said, I'm not going into that fort, you guys all go to the fort if you want to, but I'm going to watch my garden. I don't want the cows and everything to get into my garden and ruin it. I've got a good garden this year. So she stayed out there and watched her garden and all the other people that were afraid went into the fort. And the old lady rolling would take him some milk, some cottage cheese and butter, vegetables from her garden every now and then. And she'd always say, well, what are you so scared about? There aren't any Indians around here. There's no Indian trouble. What's the matter with you anyway? Well, the man rode on to Fort Walla Walla and he'll soon be back with the army. I know he will. Oh, she said, there's no trouble. We had a little skirmish up there in Spokane and a little skirmish over at Steptoe and Colonel Steptoe went on back down to Walla Walla. I don't know what's the matter with you guys. Joseph had his trouble and he's back on the reservation now. So I'm just going to stay right on my place and you can just eat my vegetables this fall if you're going to let yours go to waste.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: So they finally, after a long time, when they came back, but they were real scared. They weren't going to stay in those homesteads if the Indians were around. But grandma and the old lady rolling, they weren't a bit afraid. Grandma told the story when she was a little girl to me. One day she said, you know, the Indians never hurt anybody. When we were almost out of food and didn't have a thing to eat at all and grandpa was laying in bed with a broken leg, the Indians came down and brought us salmon, a hunch of venison, and they got wood for us and they helped us all they could. Even hunted up our lost cattle and brought them in for us. Now I don't think Indians that do that would ever hurt anybody… well, she said way back a long time ago, back in Indiana, the Indians would come up from the Platte River where they lived in their little sod house and they'd come and bring them fish and things from the river and sometimes a hunch of venison. But she said every time they'd come, my mom and them,… ollie and little baby Eldon would be hiding out in the cornfield because they didn't want to get near the Indians. But grandma Maxwell wasn't a bit afraid and neither was grandpa Maxwell and grandpa Palmer and the rest of them weren't a bit afraid either.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: We still have friends amongst the Indians. Antoinette Lewis was 16 and she would soon be the princess of the Dakota Indians. She was there in Oregon, her folks were working in the hops and in the beans, picking beans and grandpa and I were picking beans too. We had, he had decided to work at the hop yard for a while, it was easier work and I went on out to the bean patch and Antoinette said, well can I go along with you? I want to pick some beans too. Well I was glad to have her company, she was a pretty girl. I drove the car out to the bean patch and we'd pick beans all day and then when we got tired of picking beans and the rest of the crew would quit, we'd check in our beans and see how much we had and then we'd go on our way home. And on our way home we had to go buy a huge patch of nice blackberries, they called them Oregon blackberries, some were Himalayas and some were just the regular old big blackberries and we would stop and pick some berries. I didn't know very much about picking blackberries but Antoinette said I'll show you. She got a board about 12 inches wide and about as tall as she was and she'd walk up on that board clear up in the top of the bushes and she'd get berries and we had all the black berries we could possibly use and I canned some, made some jam and jelly besides. And then on the way home one day there was a place where there was some nice sweet corn and I went over to the house and asked if I could get some and he said just help yourself, take what you want because it soon be too ripe and I can't sell it anyway. I'll just give you and the Indian girl all you can carry home. So we got big armfuls of corn and took them over and put them under the fence and I said I'd buy the patch of Oregon plums, wild plums. I said well I'm going to see if I can find some wild plums so Antoinette come along with me. We got our pockets full of plums and some in our hands and we went on back and I wasn't going to crawl through that fence or go way back to the gate. I decided I'd just play it a little bit easy. I walked up at the cattle chute where they loaded cattle. I walked up on top of that and I thought well it's only just a little ways down and I'll jump down. I jumped down all right and I lit right on my back. Come to find out it was a good six feet up to the top of that chute where I jumped off. Well I laid there for a little while and Antoinette was real scared. She thought I was hurt but I wasn't very bad. I got over it in a few minutes and drove on home. The next day I didn't feel much like picking beans but we went anyway and we got beans. Then there's another place where we could get blackberries so we explored that up along the river the Willamette River and it was beautiful patch of berries there but they'd gone and scattered mosquito poison all over the thing. Little black powdery stuff that killed the mosquitoes but it was all over the berries.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Antoinette's mother Mrs. Lewis said well I don't think that'll hurt them we'll pick them anyway. Well I didn't want any of them and we Antoinette and her mother went to work picking the berries and I went on up farther. I was trying to find a place where we could get some milk and I finally found a place and went on in and asked the lady and she was a school teacher. Well she says sure you can get milk here I'll give you some. So every day then after that we went up to her place to get a quart of milk or so. And in her orchard I saw my first fig tree. The leaves were big as big as my two hands put together and the fruit was yellow and oh it had a delightful fresh flavor but they weren't any good picked off the trees they were only good if they landed on the ground first. And you picked them up but when you picked them up you had to be real careful not to get a yellow jacket in them because the yellow jackets would crawl way down inside of them to get the nectar.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: But we ate figs then every day we had our figs and we'd go after our milk and then the lady said out in my pasture there's some good Himalaya berries that's a kind of a blackberry that's as big as your thumb or a little bigger they sometimes grow as much as an inch and a half long and a half inch wide but they're awfully good. So I went on out there and she says watch out for the cattle when they come down because they aren't used to you. Well I watched for the cattle but I never did see any and we got blackberries out there and they're oh they were so good with the cream off of the milk and we just really enjoyed ourselves. And around behind Mrs. Hayner she was the boss of the her husband was the boss of a… hop mill there where they were picking the hops and milling the hops. And around her corner of her house she had a artichoke. These were the kind that grew great big buds and the artichokes were taller than my head and she says in just a week or so there'll be some rice and I'll give you some.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: I love to hear me tell this story. It was about Uncle Glenn and Uncle Claude. A way back in 1917, they had taken the herd of cattle. Well, my dad and my grandfather both had herds of cattle, and they had taken the herd out in the spring early because they were short of hay and had gone on farther on. First they were in Hatter Creek, and there they had made acquaintances with a sheep man, Cobb, and he had given them a shepherd dog, a cute little puppy named Shep. And he was a regular herd dog, and they had him and we'd go up on top of the hill sometimes and hunt huckleberries. One day we rode the horses way back up on top of the bald knob, and the huckleberries were so thick, and they were low bushes, not more than six or eight inches high, and they were so thick that the horses' hooks were just dripping huckleberry juice. We picked all we could, but we didn't have a need to carry them in. Came on back down, and on the way we saw a lost sheep. The sheep herder had gone weeks before, and this little lamb was left out there all by himself. Well, nothing to do with what we had to get that lamb, so my brother shot him, and then we had to dress him up with nothing but just a pocketknife. But he dressed him up right for him to hide away from the meat, and the meat was so good we took it back to camp and enjoyed it very much. I had been visiting the camp that weekend, and I had to go back home. We went back home, I took some of the mutton back home from mother, and mother didn't like mutton, but she thought it was maybe some wild meat, so she ate it, and oh, it was so good. And when my brother told her it was just a lamb, she said, oh, but it's the best lamb I ever ate. And then we went on over, and they took the cattle on over farther, and put her up to Hog Meadows. You know where Hog Meadows is? Well, you should. And then farther on over, clear over to Elk River and up to the basin. There they pastured the cattle on Sovereign Meadows for a while, and up on the Milwaukee Railroad, and there they were camped. Well, mom and dad and my older brother decided that they'd go up there, and I decided to go along too, but I was taking violin lessons then. I was only ten, and we had to practice a lot in order to keep up with our lessons, so I took my violin along, and my other brother took his horn along, and then we were going to have some music at the camp. The other boys had, Claude had his cello, and Glenn had his cornet or trumpet. So we went on up there, and over the hill and down to where they were, and we camped there. Just before we got into the camp, the motor in the car broke down. Well, dad says, we'll have to go back to Potlatch on the train and see if we can get a new block to put in, because that's what's the matter, and the pistons and everything to go with it. So the next day, dad and my older brother got on the train and went back to Potlatch to see if they could get a new motor. Well, they got the motor, and on the way back, they'd missed the train some way, and all the way from Bovill to Elk River, they had to borrow a hand car and pump all the way up over the Neva Hill through the tunnel and coast down to Elk River, and that's the way they got down there. But then they walked out to the camp and took their horses back and got the motor to put it together. But in the meantime, we'd been there a whole week. For my entertainment, the ranger had a daughter, and she was a little sim, and she thought, oh, it would be so interesting to play with another little girl. Well, his daughter was about 15, and I was only 10, just coming 11. And we went horseback riding, and I used one of my brother's yellow horses, and we rode around all over the place. And one day, we went with Mr. Sotter, the ranger, over to Elk Falls, Elk River Falls. It was the most beautiful falls I had ever seen. One day, I'd like to go back. And while we were there, he caught a patient, we had trout, and he said, well, I'll catch enough so your mother can have a sample of trout, real trout. So he caught a nice big mess of trout and put them in his pack sack. And then when we come home that night, when he gave mother the trout, and he said, your daughter is a very good rider. We'll take her again next time. We were going out with some wire over to another place over on top of Elk Mountain. And she can go along. So I got to go along again. We went by that beautiful falls again, and another lower falls, and up over to the timber to a pretty meadow, and up a high mountain, up way up on top. And they carried the wire on the mules, and the men put the wire up on the trees. The funniest arrangement you ever saw. They put a wire up on the tree and fastened a little circle. And then they put the wire, telephone wire, through that circle. It was easy doing, and they just did it right from their horses. And the pack animals would just keep walking along, and that wire would train out behind them into those circles that they wired up on the tree. Insulators, I think my brother told me there were. And they got up on top of the mountain. That was the end of the trail. Then they had a telephone, and then they could talk clear back down to Elk River and to Bovill and clear over into Potlatch. But the main ranger station then, it was PFI, Potlatch Timber Protective Association. And their main place to call would be down the Clarkia, which was a little ways away from Elk River, down across the hills there somewhere. I don't know where now. But anyway, that's where it went. Gold Creek, I think they said it was, and Saint Maries. And the main ranger station is at Saint Maries even today. But that was way back in 1917. Then one day, Mom said, well, you can go over and stay with Miss Stoddard. Her name was Delva Stoddard, and you can stay with her all day long, because you're getting tired of staying around here, and they're fixing on the motor. And tomorrow, we'll probably be heading back home to Moscow and Viola. So I went over and stayed the day with Delva. She had to go and get garbage for her chickens and a hog that they raised. So we got on the big wagon with a team, went down to the boarding houses in Elk River, and collected bread. Oh, she had barrels of bread. They didn't eat much bread. It seemed like they wasted more than they ate. But they had lots of bread for her chickens and some meat scraps and potato peelings and different things. And she went by the cookhouse, and the cookhouse man gave her a great big box of bread and cookies and different things. And you've got company, so they gave us some donuts and a pie. And we took those on home, and we got home. She fed her chickens. And she said, well, we'll see what we've got in our garden. She picked some peas, and there was carrots and some little tiny potatoes. She had quite a nice little garden there. And then we went in the house, and well, we've got to have something to eat along with us. So we went into the cellar. What a cellar. It was a great big, long cellar, and just lined with glass jars of meat. There was bear meat and elk meat and deer meat and fish and pheasants. And well, I just can't name it. Everything, vegetables and all kinds of things. Mr. Sodder Delva's dad was a great hand to cook and can things. And he had just about everything, and canned wild fruit jelly. I think it was elderberry and huckleberry and all kinds of things like that. And the best thing he had, he opened a can of the berry jelly, thimble berry jelly. And it was so good. And he said, well, we'll have something else. So he opened a can of grouse and the grouse breast. And we had grouse and chickens. And then we had our donuts and our pie. And he got some milk from his cow. And he had it cold in the cellar. And there was cream and butter. I don't know, but I guess maybe I was hungry. And I ate and ate and ate. And I enjoyed that meal so much. Well, he said, we'll send some back to the camp for your mother. So we brought back butter and canned huckleberries and jelly and a can of grouse and a can of deer meat that he had made. And oh, it was good. And of all things, canned peaches. He sent us two cans of peaches. So we had a real feast that night for supper at Mr.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Sodder's picnic that he gave us. That night we were playing. And I was practicing my lesson. And I was playing and playing. And the songs we liked then were the songs that were brand new. And I was playing over there, over there. And then I was playing the one about Longboy and some others. Pretty soon we looked up and there was a whole row of section workers. We called them dagos then. But they were all lined up on the crel fence just outside of our tent listening. Well, we played and played until I got so tired I couldn't play anymore. So I put my violin away and the boys played a little while longer. And then we didn't go home until we quit. They really enjoyed it. The next day, they knew we were about ready to go home. So the next day the cook came over and brought a great big huckleberry cobbler for us to eat. And they brought over jars of huckleberries for us to take home. And then the boys got interested. And while they were there, after we had already gone home, they went and brought jars at the store and sugar and canned huckleberries. They brought home six dozen quarts of canned huckleberries with sugar in. Well, now in 1917, sugar was pretty scarce and you didn't get very much. But they got it there from the logging camp. While they were there, the Fourth of July came on and the celebration. There was all kinds of logger activities. And then some people had brought in some race horses. They were going to have horse races. Well, the boys heard about it and Glenn had Patsy. She was a Bell Founder, Hamiltonian mayor and real fast. And she had a colt called Shammy. Well, Shammy was only just a youngster then. He was still nursing his mother and he was just a real up and going colt. Glenn said, Well, I'm going to enter this horse in the race and you riding. I'll keep Shammy back here at the camp. And you know what Patsy will do when you turn her loose. She'll come home. And so you ride Patsy in that race. Well, they entered the race and everybody got all ready to run. And they said, Oh, boy, cowboy can't do anything. He's got two heavier saddle and his horse isn't trained to run anyway. Well, the boys just kept still and they were going to see what they could do. Well, the race came off, the gun went off and Patsy went off too. She went home to that little colt of hers and she went. He just kept going and she got ahead of everybody else and all the other horses. And she left. She didn't stop till she got her back to camp. And then Glenn decided that he'd better take her back. So he led it back with his other horse that he had back to the starting line. And they said, Well, your horse won way ahead of all the others. They had won the race. Well, that only started the trouble. Their horses were way ahead of the other. And there was some jealous people and the boys didn't think anything about it. And Glenn went somewhere that day and Claude was around and didn't seem to make any difference much. And all of a sudden they missed the horses. They were all gone but one old bird. Old bird was a welch pony and a wonderful pony at that. She'd track the other horses anywhere. Well, Glenn got on the horse on bird and he said, Bird, go find the horses. And he rode and rode and it got dark. And he wondered about Claude back there at camp. But Claude was taking care of the chores and doing things and worrying about Glenn. But Glenn kept right on riding and he noticed there was wagon tracks and the horses were right behind the wagon. They were leading those horses away, stealing them in other words. Well, that was a new kind of a horse. Glenn didn't know what to think about it. He had his gun and his saddle and his pony. But he was going to get those horses or else. So he rode on into the night and he come to a fence and he opened the fence and left it open and went on through. Pretty soon he saw a little light in the distance. So he got off his horse and he crawled up, creeped real carefully. He didn't know what to do, but he didn't want to leave Bird. So he put his hand over Bird's nose and got up close and he saw his horses. They were all tied up there. So he cut them all loose and he and Bird and their horses slipped out and went back to camp just as hard as they could go after they got out through. Well, the people never came back to the camp to get those horses. But that wasn't the end of all their troubles they had up there at Elk River. The fire broke out and it burned and burned. Of course, this was the second year they'd been up there. So they were well acquainted with the country and the sheep men were up in there too. But it was good pasture and they were there and the fire came out. The ranger came by and he said, you'd better get your cattle out while you can. That fire is going to be over Neva Pass before you get there. Well, Dad had a bull we called Old Joe. He wore a bell and he led the cattle everywhere. So Glenn said, let's go. They got all packed up and they put their gear in behind the cattle and they followed. Glenn went ahead and led one of the cows and Old Joe followed and they went down the road. They got to the fire. Glenn had to go back to see about things, but Old Joe just shook his head and plowed right on through. Glenn went back to help with the horses and the drag and they went on through and up over Neva Pass and down on the other side. Glenn looked back and said there was the sheep. The sheep man was following right behind one just as close as they could come. And they went out of there. The Old Joe led them through around through the trails and down to the creek, the Ruby Creek. And the cattle stopped and got a little drink and went on through. But Joe was going home. He shook his horns and shook his bell and the other cattle started bawling. And they followed him right on down through. And they came to Bovill and they went right through Bovill. Old Joe went right through the mayor's yard and took the sweet pea fence along on his horns. They didn't even stop down at Hog Meadows. They just kept right on going. Well, the boys finally got ahead of them and rounded them up and they stopped overnight down at the end of Hog Meadows for that night. Then the next day they came on down. They called up dad in the meantime and dad met them and helped them. And they got home in a hurry that time with the cattle. Turned them out on the stubble fields and that was the end of the Elk River episode. They never went back to Elk River again. The next year they took the herd, I think about 90 some head of cattle and some horses, up into what's Big Creek now. They built some fences and they had the horses in there and the cattle. And that was where they finally wound up with the… 1937. The years that Lillian A. Maxwell, our cousin, graduated from high school at Kamiah, she came up and stayed with us for a while. She wanted to go out to the cattle camp where the boys were in the cattle. So I went with her and we went up on the motorcycle that my brother had. He had a sidecar on it and we could ride in the sidecar.
