So we went up to the cattle camp and they had fixed a shed up there and they had made a kind of a part of a log cabin where they kept their feed and things. And they pitched a tent up for us so that we girls could stay in that pen there. And Glenn had given me his rifle and he said, now look, if you hear anything in the night, don't shoot but wait until you see what it is first because we've got cougars around here. Well, there was a pair of cougars that lived there in the head of the meadow there on Big Creek. And that night, sure enough, they commenced to howl. Way over on the hill you could hear one and then on the other hill you could hear the other. And then you'd hear the coyotes and then the cougar. The next morning my other brother had come in and dad and they said, well, we're going to see if we can't get that cougar. So they took their rifles but they left the 32 with me. I had learned to shoot in the meantime so that I could shoot pretty fair. Now look, she said, if you see that fellow, you shoot him. Well, I feel feeling pretty bad. I had some boiled food that morning for breakfast and my stomach was all upset and I was laying in bed and I said, yes, I would. And my horse Pete was just a paw in a circle all around. She just didn't want to stay there one bit. She was an Arabian pony and well horse mare, I guess you'd better call her because she was about 700 pounds and just a real good saddle horse. But she didn't like it up there in the mountains. She could smell the bear and the cougar. I heard the boys up in the mountains. Pretty soon I heard them shout and I heard some shots. And I crawled out from under the tent to look out over the meadow and I saw a yellow street going across bound, bound, bound. There was the cougar, biggest line. Well, I got scolded when they came back. Why didn't you shoot him? Well, I just didn't. That was all I could say. The next day, Lillian and I went out for the roundup and then she decided she'd go out with the groceries with Glenn on the motorcycle and I stayed in camp. So I went out with my other brother and dad to round up some streets. We went up past the Last Chance Creek and on up to Lost Meadow and Black Meadow. And I said, well, I'm going to go on back to camp and I'll go down this way. If I see any streets, I'll bring them on down. Dad said, all right, we'll look around a little bit more up in here. Glenn ought to be back by the time you get down there. I started down the trail and I just went propping along. I was riding old Betty, a little bay cow pony that was very, very gentle and well, she was trustworthy, dad said. He wouldn't let me ride Pete because she wasn't trustworthy in the mountains. So Pete stayed at camp and went round and round on her picket pen until she wore a trail about a foot deep around that end of that picket line. She was restless and she wanted to get out of there. Dad said, well, you're going to have to take her home when you go home, that's sure, because she just simply won't stay up here. Well, on the way home, I didn't see anything and I didn't hear anything and it was just all easy going. There was beautiful orchids blooming in the grass and along the side of the duff underneath the trees. There was trilliums and white star flowers, lots of orchids and other kind of flowers and I was interested in them. I didn't even see a pheasant or hear a twig drop. We just kept plodding on down until we got home. When we got home, I got Vinnie in and tied Betty up and took the saddle off and looked around. Glenn hadn't got in yet. I was all by myself. I didn't like that too well, but I was there. So I got my rifle and went inside my tent and laid down to rest in the lounge because I was pretty tired. And then pretty soon I heard Dad shouting, here come Dad and my other brother. And they said, well, did you see anything? Not a thing. I said, did you hear anything? Nope, didn't hear anything. Dad said, well, you carry that rifle here after or you're not going to ride up here. Do you know what we saw following you down the trail? Right in your horse tracks? That cougar. He was covering Betty's tracks right along all the way down to within a quarter of a mile of camp. Now you either go home on peat in the morning or you carry the rifle. Well, I was about ready to go home anyway. I just about had enough. I was tired and round up was over with anyway. They'd be driving out the next few days, maybe a week later.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: He'd ride one of the horses and I'd ride Pete. Betty had to go home because she was getting a little bit lame and Dad thought I should take her home anyway. So we started out. And Dad says, now you be sure and go up over that hill by Johnson's. It's only three miles farther and you'll go that way because Malcolm is mad enough. He got after Glenn and the boys here the other day and Claude and Tommy had an awful practice with him. He was going to beat Claude over the head and Tommy made him stop with the rifle. And that was just about enough. We can't have any more trouble like that. So you go home with Louie and you go around by Johnson's. That's an order. All right. But I don't like that makes it just that much farther home. Well, you go on now and behave. All right. I started down the road on Pete and Louie came along on Betty. We got down to the corner to go up over the hill to Johnson's. I said, Louie, I'm not going to go that extra three miles. I'm going through. You coming? I kicked Pete in the ribs and we sailed over the fence and away we went. Right on down as fast as we could go through Malcolm and on down to Bill Texas. We got down there. I stopped, pulled up a little bit to let the horses heave a little bit. And Louie says, boy, did I ever ride. I had to to keep up with you. You're flying on that, Mayor. But he says, I don't know what the old man's going to say, but there wasn't anybody around to see us. And we got out of there before they did see us. Well, I said, that's the way it is. Let's go home. So we rode on down the road until we got to Harvard and stopped there and got a little bite to eat and went on down. We stopped at his place, the Gilder Place. And just before you get into Harvard, it's I think the Gilder Place belongs to order now, but I'm not too sure that that's where he stops. He went on into his folks and I rolled on down home, past Princeton and on down, crossed over the hill.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Flanagan Road home. Well, we rested at home and it wasn't more than a week. And Dad came down and he says, you've got to take a couple of horses back up. So you start out Sunday morning and you take those horses and have those. And Tammy and Betty, you ride Pete if you want those things. You don't like to ride the others, but you take those two horses and go back up there. And this time no more going around by Malcolm's. You go over the hill to Johnson's. I'll be waiting up there for you so we can take you down across the hill. I'm afraid of that. What that Malcolm will do to you. Well, I rode on up. It was quite a ways. I started just after daylight. Took a lunch this time so I wouldn't have to stop and kept the horses at a good fast trot most of the way. When we got up to Sexton's, we stopped and he says, where you going, sis? You're going up by Malcolm's this time again. And he laughed. He were a great big six foot two man and he probably weighed about 250 and he had a great big song bro, the old fashioned kind. And he had high heeled cowboy boots that he always wore and he rode a big black stallion with white feet and a blaze in his forehead. And he just got through with his round up. He says, if you're going to go up to Malcolm's, I'd better ride along and see him pick up the pieces. Oh, I said, I don't think he's the bad guy. Yeah, not if he's the bad guy. Just arrested his son for poaching and maybe the old man's cooled off a little bit. You better go on around. Your dad's waiting up there at Johnson's for you. Well, I said, okay. Well, he says, you better do it, sis. Old Mr. Sexton, Bill Sexton always called me sis for some reason or other. I didn't realize at that time that he was relative of ours, but he was.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: His mother's mother was Grandpa Maxwell's sister, Mary Chambers. And Bill Sexton's wife was her daughter. So actually he was a, they were cousins of ours, I suppose. Anyway, we went, I went up around the road and gave my horses a drink and got them to go on a good fast clip and I got up to that road. Oh, it looks so good to go right straight on up the creek instead of go around and up over that hill. I wondered if I dared do it. And I got there and Betty stuck up her nose and decided she was going and old Shammy says, come on, we're going. They'd been up there so much it was getting home. So, Shammy was good going and so was Betty. And they started out and kind of hard to turn. So I just let them go. What come naturally. I didn't want to go around anyway. So we rode on up the road at a good fast lope and there wasn't a gate shut. There was a new road cleared around his place. And old Malcolm's place over in the hill was, we didn't even have to go by it. So I rode right straight on up last chance and up to round middle and camp. I got there and pretty soon here come dad down over the hill. And he says, you came straight through. Bill told me you did. Yes, I said I did. The horses didn't want to turn. They wanted to go straight up. Well, he says, I guess they did. Shammy and Betty don't like it up here and you didn't bring Pete this time. Well, that's good. Well, he says, Ben will take you home now. So you hike on. He's all ready to go on the bike. So he came back over the hill. Glenn had been waiting up at Johnson's. So he came back and got me and we went right on down past old Malcolm's place and down past Sexton's and Sexton's stopped. And he said, well, I see you got through all right. He says, I was kind of worried. So I went up to tell your dad you've gone through. I said, you did. And he said, I did. Well, he says, goodbye, sis. I guess you'll be going to school now. I said, I think this is about the last of the roundup for me this year. So we went on back home on the motorcycle. Another story I could tell you was a little bit different. We were on the drag driving over the hill to Brown's Meadow. The calves were all ahead and the calves were little and pokey. It was early in the spring, but it was still good weather. It was first of May. And then going up the Flanagan Hill, just leaving the Flanagan Creek, Betty got loose from the wagon and started back. Well, then, yell, get on your horse and go get her. So I got on Pete, who'd been tied to the wagon too. And I started after her. I was sure I could catch her because Pete did outrun Betty most any time.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Well, I run and I run and I run. And we went down across Flanagan Creek and up the hill past Pixley's and on down across… where the hog farm is and then started up the next hill. And we got clear over to where you go up past the hill up toward, oh, it was a good steep hill anyway, and it was all clay. There was a way up ahead was a teamster and a big load of logs. Wood, he was hauling wood. I recognized who it was. It was Hill. So I yelled and I said, head that horse off for me, will you please? I can't catch her. He turned around and he cracked his whip right in front of Betty's nose and climbed down and caught her. He'd caught her with the whip around her head and nose some way. Anyway, he had her caught and I ran in. He said, you couldn't catch that little short headed ... on with that long legged Arabian mare of yours? Ha ha ha, he laughed at me. Well, I said, I just couldn't. I guess she wanted to go home. He says, I guess she did. Look at her. She's sweating all over and your horse is sweating too. Why couldn't you catch that little horse, little pony with that Arabian mare? Oh, he says, he laughed at me. I guess they both wanted to go home anyway. Now you have to go back, huh? I said, yes, I'll have to go back and they're going up the hill. They'll be over to Brown's Meadow before I catch him at this rate. Well, he says, you better get going. And so I got the horses and this time I tied Betty on with a rope around her neck and tied her to the back of my saddle by the saddle strings. So that she'd be able to keep her distance from the fight. Mr. Hill told me how to do it, so I did and away we went. And we looked all the way down and up the hill and down another hill. Got clear over to Meeks' Mill and started on down and still no cattle heard. I was following and I knew. But you know, actually, they were clear over there past the Flanagan and over into the Rock Creek country and they were going over just about two miles from Brown's Meadow by the time I caught up with them. Oh, I was disgusted. Why didn't Pete run fast enough to catch Betty? I just couldn't figure that out. But I guess Pete didn't want to go back up there anyway. She didn't like the woods ever and she didn't like the cattle, which was just against her religion. One job I didn't like was herding the cattle and bringing them in off the stubble in the fall when they brought the cattle in off the rain. They'd always get stubble pasture from some of the neighbors around. One time, especially, I was riding a welch pony. I think this time I was about eight or nine years old. And I had gone up in the field to get the cattle. They were on Uncle Wes's 80 acres. There's a nice field up in there. But I don't know why it happened to me, but it did. There was some holes in the hill on the top of the hill there that looked really interesting. I got off of my horse and went down to look down into those holes. I dropped some sticks and things down in the holes and all of a sudden my horse snorted and I grabbed the reins and she jerked me back. And there was a badger. It was a badger hole and there was the badger. Well, I threw some clods at him and he went down the hole again, but I got on my horse and went on after the cattle. But that was the first time I had ever seen a badger. My horse was afraid of them. Later I was told that horses are really afraid of badgers because they make holes in the horses and step in them and break their legs. But I was herding the cattle that afternoon. It was Sunday and I had to go all the way over and stay with them and keep them out of the railroad track. There was Uncle Wes's garden and I had to keep them out of that. And there was a berry patch. Oh, there was the best berries there and peaches and different things and I could eat those. I took some potatoes out of the garden, went over by the trees, built me a little fire and roasted my potatoes. In the meantime, the cattle were scattering and I had to run fast and get them off the railroad track. But this time, for some reason or other, I didn't get them all. And one or two of them were gone and I hunted and hunted and I couldn't find them. Finally it was time to take them home so I took them back home and told Dad that there was two of them gone, Little Dory and Old Dory. Little Dory was a black heifer with a white face and Old Dory was a yellow cow with a white face. Well, he took his horse and went to find them and he didn't find them and he couldn't. He looked and he looked. He finally found them up on the railroad track. But a train had come by and bruised up one of them pretty bad but didn't kill her. But he brought them on home then. But he said, now you don't do that anymore. Well, I didn't. But when I brought them back, I had to take them up into the pasture and there was a big spring there and there was water. The boys were supposed to pump it full of water for the cattle but I was to keep the cattle away from it until they kind of laid down, chewed their cuddles a while so they wouldn't bloat because there was alfalfa there too. But they didn't. One time one slipped away and got up in the pasture and she died a bloat. Dad said, well, it's just too much for a little girl to herd those cattle. We got to have somebody else doing it. So that was the last I had to herd those cattle. But talking about bloat, it was bad business that fall. Mr. Gray, our neighbor, had quite a dairy herd and he was pasturing on alfalfa. Dad told him it was bad business. They'd bloat, no, they'll be all right. He said, but the next day we heard a racket down there and he was running these cattle up and down.

speaker: Verna Palmer Hardt
words: Our hired girl Myrtle that had stayed with us for years, brother, was the veterinarian for the community, saw what was happening.
